title: California nursing homes manipulate size thresholds to avoid staffing rules, limiting access for disadvantaged patients
source_unit: California nursing-home facilities, bed-count threshold, staffing requirements, facility size manipulation, and patient access

observations.period: Working paper issued October 2026; California nursing homes with at least 100 beds

denominator.unit: California nursing-home facilities and patients; exact sample count not disclosed in the NBER abstract

threshold_bunching.unit: extensive bunching occurs in response to additional staffing requirements for facilities with at least 100 beds

above_threshold_staffing.unit: higher staffing above the threshold is nearly entirely due to selection rather than a causal staffing increase

size_manipulation.unit: low-staffing facilities manipulate their size to avoid the regulation

patient_access.unit: size distortions limit access, particularly for disadvantaged patients

observations.method: The paper develops a treatment-effects estimator for threshold-based regulations under precise manipulation, decomposing facilities into response types using counterfactual and realized staffing and size to separate causal effects from selection.
observations.uncertainty: The NBER abstract does not disclose facility or patient counts, effect sizes, the exact access measure, follow-up window, or the full identification assumptions. The paper is a working paper; the abstract does not establish clinical outcomes, worker conditions, prices, profits, or whether the access limitation persists after the observed response.
observations.subgroup: Low-staffing California nursing homes near the 100-bed threshold and disadvantaged patients affected by size distortions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Facilities may change ownership, services, admissions, bed counts, staffing composition, or reporting rather than improve or reduce care in one common way; measured access can reflect facility selection, local capacity, patient sorting, payer mix, and other responses to regulation.

related_sources.claim: Nursing homes respond strategically to inspections, and inspection ratings predict relative patient mortality despite not measuring absolute quality cleanly.
Nursing-home mergers reduce deficiency citations and direct-care hours, with compliance improvements concentrated in low-severity categories.
Detailed nursing-home financial evidence reports widespread related-party tunneling and a large gap between reported and implied investment returns.

boundary: This record adds a firm-response and consumer-access layer to the US nursing-home regulation chain. It does not disclose effect sizes or establish clinical harm, worker outcomes, price effects, ownership effects, or a universal response to staffing regulation outside California nursing homes.
